title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, illegally deported by the Trump administration, arrives in Spain after voluntarily leaving the US | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whom the Trump administration illegallydeportedto El Salvador last year as part of its immigration crackdown, arrived in Spain Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the US.

Abrego Garcia and his wife, who is an American citizen, arrived in Madrid on a commercial flight Wednesday morning. Abrego Garcia entered Spain on a tourist visa, allowing a visit of only up to 90 days.

At a press conference hours after his arrival, Abrego Garcia said he was “happy because this time I am leaving with my freedom, and I am not leaving the way they removed me before, in a practically inhumane manner.”

“I have many options for my future; we have not chosen yet. My family and I will choose the next steps,” he said.

Abrego Garcia is scheduled to speak at several events in Spain and other countries in the days ahead. His departure comes after the Salvadoran national who was living in Maryland became the face of the administration’s aggressive deportation campaign last spring.

The Department of Homeland Security announced his departure from the US on Tuesday, with Secretary Markwayne Mullin writing on social media that he was “delighted” by the man’s move to self-deport.

We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Abrego Garcia and his family, confirmed he had left, saying in a statement that he “walked out of the United States a free man.”

ICE agents had removed his ankle monitor at Washington Dulles airport Tuesday night.

One of his lawyers, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said Abrego Garcia had left the US because he thought he was “never going to get a fair shake” under the Trump administration despite being married to a US citizen. “He has legal migration options available under law that this administration is never going to give him,” he said.

“But you know what, he’s going to outlast this administration. Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to last a lot longer than Donald Trump,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added. “And he will be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident under the next administration.”

Abrego Garcia entered the US illegally around 2011, but in 2019 an immigration judge barred his removal to El Salvador after finding a gang there had been “targeting him and threatening him with death because of his family’s pupusa business.”

Despite that order, he was arrested by US officials last March and flown to El Salvador, where he was detained ata notorious mega prison. The Trump administration later admitted incourt documentshe was deported due toa clerical error.

A federal judge ordered the administration to work to bring him back stateside, but officials resisted for months.

The administration eventually partnered with El Salvador to return him last June. He was arrested on human smuggling charges when he returned to American soil – but a federal judgedismissed those in Maythis year, citing a “tainted investigation” by Attorney General Todd Blanche.

The government appealed that ruling, vowing to deport Abrego Garcia to a third country in Africa, such as Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, or, most recently suggested, Liberia, according to the Associated Press.

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who flew to El Salvador and met Abrego Garcia at the Cecot prison while pushing for his release last year, welcomed the news of his voluntary departure.

“A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” he wrote in astatementon Tuesday. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity.”

He added he was relieved Abrego Garcia would be free “from this Administration’s constant persecution.”

The Democratic senator said at a later press conference that the administration “did not succeed at what they wanted to do.”

President Donald Trump launched his immigration crackdown almost immediately after taking office for his second term, promising to deport a million people in his first year. While officials didn’t reach this number – the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported 605,000 deportations in 2025 – the aggressive campaign shook the nation, with ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) raids across the country and thedeployment of the National Guard.

The White House hasintentionally retreatedfrom its in-your-face approach after confrontations between federal and state officials in multiple states. During clashes in Minneapolis earlier this year, video of masked agents killing protesters sparked outrage and protest.

Butimmigration enforcementis still happening nationwide – just more below-the-radar now, under border czar Tom Homan. In recent months, the DHS has awarded a nearly$1.3 billioncontract for ICE deportation flights; at least $1.5 billion for border infrastructure; amultimillion-dollarcontract to transport ICE detainees; and nearly$13 millionfor a canine facility.

In a post on social media, DHS said: “It’s not surprising this criminal illegal alien would choose to go to Spain, a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens. Spain’s radical open-border policies have made the once-great country a breeding ground for illegal migrants. Good riddance.”

CNN has reached out to the DHS for further comment, as well as the Department of Justice and Abrego Garcia’s attorneys.

After his return to the US, Abrego Garcia continued fighting the threat of deportation. He had previously said he would have preferred to be sent to Costa Rica, a country that has said it would be willing to give him some form of legal status.

However, he was unable to voluntarily leave to Costa Rica due to release conditions imposed by the federal judge who dismissed the criminal charges against him in May.

Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, also said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States,” according to the Associated Press.

Instead, Lyons argued, Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the US has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals, Lyons wrote.

The case took an unusual turn onOctober 6when, shortly before a hearing to determine whether ICE could deport him to Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia, according to the Associated Press.

They returned 15 minutes later, and the hearing was canceled; both sides gathered for another 90 minutes before they left the courthouse. No explanation was given; Abrego Garcia’s attorney only said the court case was not ready to proceed, according to the Associated Press.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Kaanita Iyer and Mauricio Torres contributed to this report.

CNN’s Kaanita Iyer and Mauricio Torres contributed to this report.
